fixes.row: verb: “Having been sanctified”, “you were sanctified”  /  “Being sanctified”, “sanctify you completely”, “let the holy continue to be holy”
fixes.why: Two faults. (1) Rule 6: the first label's quoted phrase “Having been sanctified” is in none of its eight verses (Heb 10:10 says “we have been sanctified”; Acts 20:32, Acts 26:18 and 1 Cor 1:2 say “those sanctified” / “all who are sanctified”, which in English is not past; 2 Tim 2:21 makes it follow “if anyone cleanses himself”). (2) The sort is not by the Greek form, as the spec's _why says: John 17:19 (ex-hagiasmenoi, perfect) and 1 Cor 1:2 / Acts 20:32 (perfect participles) stand on opposite sides, and 1 Thess 5:23 and Rev 22:11 are aorist, not present. The only principle left is the worker's reading of each verse as finished or unfinished, so the grouping itself is a reading: a Wesleyan hears “completely” filed as “ongoing”, a Reformed reader hears “you were sanctified” filed as “done”, and Acts 20:32 sits under “done” only by interpretation.
fixes.fix: Take the worker's own fallback: merge the two rows into one, in Bible order, labelled only in phrases that occur: “you were sanctified”, “we have been sanctified”, “those who are being sanctified”, “sanctify you completely”, “may be sanctified by the truth”, “let the holy continue to be holy”. Keep the no-side note on the one row, with the wording in the notes fix below. Do not label either half 'done' or 'ongoing'.

fixes.row: noun: Holiness that is God's: ... / Holiness as the aim and fruit of the life: ...
fixes.why: The quoted parts of both labels are in the verses, but the framing words are the worker's, and they line up as given-by-God versus pursued-by-us, which is the very point the traditions argue. The sort does not hold on that line: 1 Thess 3:13 (the Lord establishes your hearts in holiness) and 1 Thess 4:7 (God has called us to holiness) are God's doing yet stand in the 'of the life' row, while Heb 12:10 'that we may share in His holiness' is a purpose, not a gift already held.
fixes.fix: Drop 'that is God's' and 'aim and fruit of the life' from the two labels and keep only the quoted phrases: “share in His holiness”, “sanctified by the Spirit”, Christ “our holiness” / “pursue holiness”, “perfecting holiness”, “leads to holiness”, “called ... to holiness”. Keep the two rows side by side with the no-side note.

fixes.row: adjective: Called to be saints, called and chosen to be holy; noun and verb sanctification rows (the no-side notes)
fixes.why: The three no-side notes name different sets of positions. The adjective and noun notes say 'in Christ at once, by growth over a life, or both'; only the verb note adds 'a second crisis'. Anyone whose reading is not on the list in a given note (a further work of the Spirit, sharing in God's life through the Church and its sacraments) can fairly say that note leaves them out, and a list is a claim about what the options are.
fixes.fix: Use one wording in all three places and name no positions: 'Christian traditions part on how and when the saints are made holy. The page sets the text's verses side by side and takes no side.' (Add 'A verse that fits more than one stands in more than one.' where it applies.)

fixes.row: adjective: Called to be saints, called and chosen to be holy
fixes.why: Rule 1: four of the eight verses do not say 'called' or 'chosen'. Eph 5:27 and Col 1:22 are 'present her / present you holy'; Col 3:12 is 'the elect of God, holy and beloved'; Heb 3:1 is 'holy brothers'. The label covers only the verses that carry its words.
fixes.fix: Relabel: “Called to be saints”, “chose us ... to be holy”, “present you holy”, “holy and beloved”, “holy brothers”.

fixes.why: The grouping is right: all 89 verses were read and each carries 'Holy Spirit', none is an Old Testament verse, and Rom 15:19 is correctly kept out. The note is the trouble: 'Holy is the title ... so they are not read as verses about holiness as a quality' is the page ruling on what the word does in these verses. For a Trinitarian reader the Spirit's holiness is not set aside by the name; the sentence reads as if it were. Rule 2/1: say what the verses say and sort, do not instruct the reader how to read them.
fixes.fix: Replace the note with: 'In these verses the text calls the Spirit holy (“the Holy Spirit”). They are grouped here by that name. Where the noun is used instead -- “the spirit of Your holiness”, “the Spirit of holiness” -- see the noun section.'

fixes.row: adjective: “The Holy One”, “holy and true”: the title without a name
fixes.why: Rule 5. Six of the nine verses are Hebrew Scripture, and the row's heading carries a phrase, 'holy and true', that occurs only in Revelation. The Old Testament verses are filed under a New Testament heading (the note admits the readings differ). The Isaiah/Job/Proverbs/Hosea verses should be heard as the Hebrew's 'the Holy One' first. The note on 1 John 2:20, Rev 3:7, Rev 6:10 (Father or Christ, no choice made) is fair and should stay.
fixes.fix: Split in two. Row A: “The Holy One”: the title without a name (Job 6:10, Prov 9:10, 30:3, Isa 10:17, 40:25, Hos 11:12), note: 'The verse gives the title and no name.' Row B (New Testament, after the Jesus row): “from the Holy One”, “the One who is holy and true” (1 John 2:20, Rev 3:7, Rev 6:10) with the existing 'some readers take the Father and some Christ; the page does not choose' note.

fixes.why: The row is by hand and every verse names or plainly means Jesus, so rule 3 is kept. But a reader meets Mark 1:24 first (it is a shown example) with no hint that the speaker is an unclean spirit, and the label does not say who calls Him holy in the other six. Without it the row reads as testimony the page is offering.
fixes.fix: Add a note: 'Said of Jesus by an unclean spirit (Mark 1:24, Luke 4:34), by Peter (John 6:69), in Peter's sermon (Acts 3:14), in the church's prayer (Acts 4:27, 4:30) and by the angel to Mary (Luke 1:35).'

fixes.row: adjective: Holy angels, “holy ones”, “the saints of the Most High”
fixes.why: Rule 5 and rule 1. The heading leads with 'Holy angels', but only five of the 22 verses (Mark 8:38, Luke 9:26, Acts 10:22, Rev 14:10, and Dan 8:13's 'holy one') name angels; most are the Hebrew/Aramaic 'holy ones' whose referent the verse leaves open, and Daniel 7 is read by Jewish and many Christian readers as the people of the Most High. Leading with 'Holy angels' tilts every other verse toward the angel reading even though the note says the page does not choose. Separately, 2 Thess 1:10 says 'glorified in His saints ... by all who have believed, including you', so it names believers in the verse and does not belong with the open cases.
fixes.fix: Relabel: “holy ones”, “the saints of the Most High”; “holy angels”. Keep the existing note. Move 2 Thess 1:10 to the 'The saints' row.

fixes.why: Both lists are by hand and each verse names who acts (Heb 13:12 names Jesus; Exod 31:13 and Lev 20:8 the LORD; John 10:36 the Father), so nothing is equated by rule, and the label keeps the two apart by name. But in one row with no note it reads as one agent; John 10:36 has Jesus as the one sanctified, not the one who sanctifies; Eph 5:26 does not name Christ in the verse (5:25 does); and the Spirit, who is named as sanctifying in Rom 15:16, 1 Cor 6:11, 2 Thess 2:13 and 1 Pet 1:2, is in the 'Sanctified by' row, not here, which a Pentecostal reader will notice.
fixes.fix: Add a note: 'In each verse the text names who sanctifies: the LORD or the Father in the Old Testament verses and in John 10:36 and 1 Thess 5:23; Jesus in John 17:19, Heb 2:11 and 13:12 (and Eph 5:26, in the sentence that begins at 5:25). John 10:36 has the Father sanctifying Jesus. For the Spirit, see “Sanctified by”.'

fixes.row: adjective: Every other use (the saints verses left in the catch-all)
fixes.why: These 17 verses all print 'saints' for ἅγιοι, the same word and the same sense as the 'The saints' row, yet sit in 'Every other use'. They include the ones readers look up (the saints will judge the world, the saints' inheritance, the Spirit intercedes for the saints, the righteous acts of the saints). Splitting them off means the 'The saints' row looks like the whole of the New Testament's use of the word, and puts the verses a Catholic or Orthodox reader would want beside the rest into a heap.
fixes.fix: Move them to 'The saints' and widen the label: 'The saints: written to, greeted, served, loved and prayed for; interceded for, inheriting, judging; harmed, killed, praying, enduring'. (Matt 27:52 'many saints' may stay in the catch-all.)

fixes.row: adjective: A holy place, holy ground, the holy city, the holy mountain, the holy temple
fixes.why: Rule 5. Ten of the 32 verses are Hebrew Scripture ('eaten in a holy place', Ps 46:4), but the four examples a reader sees first are Acts 7:33, Rev 21:2, Matt 24:15, then Ps 46:4. And the row sets 1 Cor 3:17 and Eph 2:21 (the church as a holy temple) and Heb 8:2, 9:24 ('the true sanctuary', a 'copy') in a single list with the Levitical place, with nothing marking that the meaning has changed. The big noun row of 232 Hebrew-place verses is fine on its own terms; it is this adjective row that mixes.
fixes.fix: Order the examples Hebrew first (Ps 46:4, Exod 29:31, Eccl 8:10, then the New Testament), and add a note: 'The first ten are the Hebrew's “holy place”; the rest are the Greek, where the holy place, the holy city and the temple are also used of the church (1 Cor 3:17, Eph 2:21) and of the sanctuary in heaven (Heb 8:2, 9:24).'

fixes.row: adjective: Holy to the LORD: a people, a nation, priests, the Nazirite; a holy man, holy prophets and apostles  (and the noun catch-all)
fixes.why: 1 Pet 3:5 'the holy women of the past' is in the row but the label names a holy man and omits the women; Mark 6:20 is Herod's opinion and Num 16:3 is Korah's claim, so neither is 'holy to the LORD'. And the Hebrew noun's own words for the people, 'the holy seed' (Isa 6:13, Ezra 9:2) and 'the Holy People, the Redeemed of the LORD' (Isa 62:12, Dan 12:7), are in the noun section's catch-all with no pointer, so a rabbi looking for how the Hebrew calls Israel holy finds the adjective row first and these missing.
fixes.fix: Relabel: 'Called holy: a people, a nation, priests, the Nazirite; a holy man, holy women, holy prophets and apostles'. Add a note on the row: 'Num 16:3 is Korah's claim; Mark 6:20 is said of John by the narrator. The Hebrew noun also says “the holy seed” and “the Holy People”: Isa 6:13, 62:12, Ezra 9:2, Dan 12:7, under “Every other use” in the noun section.' (Better still, add those four to this row if the builder can.)

fixes.row: verb: Sanctified by: the truth, the word, faith, the blood, the sacrifice, the Spirit, a believing spouse
fixes.why: 'The blood' is one label for Heb 13:12 (Jesus' blood) and Heb 9:13 (the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer), so a reader takes the animal-blood verse as a statement about Christ's blood, and a rabbi sees the Levitical rite used as a foil without being told it is the Levitical rite. 1 Tim 4:5 is food sanctified, not a person. The 'a believing spouse' phrase is fair and the baptism question is correctly left alone.
fixes.fix: Relabel: ... “the blood of goats and bulls” (Heb 9:13, the old rites), “his own blood” (Heb 13:12), “the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ”, ... “food sanctified by the word of God and prayer” (1 Tim 4:5).

worker_points.why: Grouping and the exclusion of Rom 15:19 are right (all 89 read; each has 'Holy Spirit'; none is Old Testament). The note's 'so they are not read as verses about holiness as a quality' is a ruling on how to read; reword as in the fixes.
Fair as a by-hand row; add the who-says-it note. Mark 1:24 and Luke 4:34 are an unclean spirit's words and should be marked as such.
The note on the three New Testament verses is fair; the Hebrew verses should not sit under a heading carrying Revelation's phrase. Split.

worker_points.point: 4. 'The LORD, the Holy One of Israel' (37)
worker_points.why: All 37 read; the LORD or God is named in each or in the immediate phrase (Hos 11:9, Hab 1:12, 3:3, Isa 49:7 included). Old Testament verses only; heard on their own terms.

worker_points.point: 5. Holy angels, 'holy ones', 'the saints of the Most High' (22)
worker_points.why: The no-choice note is right but the 'Holy angels' lead heading pulls against it; relabel, and move 2 Thess 1:10.

worker_points.point: 6. Sanctification rows: does the grouping take a side?
worker_points.why: Yes. The 'done / ongoing' sort is not even by Greek form (John 17:19 and 1 Cor 1:2 are the same form on opposite sides), the first label's quoted phrase is in none of its verses, and the noun pair's 'God's' versus 'of the life' lines up with the monergism/synergism divide. Merge the verb pair, strip the framing from the noun pair, unify the note.
Leaving the children and baptism alone is right. The 'the blood' label hides that Heb 9:13 is animal blood; relabel.

Not equated by rule (lists by hand; each verse names the agent; label keeps the names). It needs a who-acts note, because John 10:36 has Jesus as the one sanctified and the Spirit as sanctifier is in another row.

worker_points.point: 9. 'Hallow the name ... sanctify Christ as Lord' (19)
worker_points.why: 1 Pet 3:15 and Isa 8:13 are each in the row by their own words; the label equates neither. Matt 6:9 and Luke 11:2 are shown first, but Isa 8:13 and Isa 29:23 are next and Old Testament verses make up most of the row.

worker_points.point: 10. 'The LORD our God is holy', 'Holy Father', 'Holy is His name'
worker_points.why: Examples and all 20 verses fit; Rev 3:7 and 6:10 are kept out, John 17:11 and Luke 1:49 are in on their own words.

worker_points.point: 11. 'The saints' (Protestant vs Catholic and Orthodox use)
worker_points.why: 'Saints' as the Berean prints it, with the verse describing what is done, is the right line. But 17 'saints' verses are left in 'Every other use' (1 Cor 6:2, Eph 1:18, Rom 8:27, Col 1:12, Rev 19:8 among them); move them in.

worker_points.point: 12. 'Prepare for battle' etc. (5) folded into the verb catch-all
worker_points.why: A true-to-text point (the Hebrew is the verb for sanctify), not a doctrinal one; the five verses are in the catch-all and do no harm there.

worker_points.point: 13. Hebrew 'holy mountain' in the noun section, Greek 'holy city' in the adjective section
worker_points.why: The _about says the sections follow the part of speech, and the 232-verse noun row is entirely Hebrew place language, heard on its own terms, with the holy/common distinction (Lev 10:10, Ezek 44:23, Ezek 22:26) in 'What is made holy' where the priestly material belongs. The mixing fault is in the adjective place row (see fixes); the large noun row needs nothing.

missing.what: Ps 16:10, 'Your Holy One' (Hebrew chasid, the verse Acts 2:27 and 13:35 quote with ὅσιος). It is in neither the chasid list under 'other words' nor anywhere in the hub, so the reader who follows Acts 2:27 back finds no Hebrew counterpart. Add it to the chasid verses with the note that the Berean prints 'Your Holy One' here, not 'saints'.

Pointer from the 'Holy to the LORD: a people' row to the Hebrew noun's 'the holy seed' / 'the Holy People' now in the noun 'Every other use' row (see fixes), so the Hebrew's own naming of Israel as holy is not hidden by the part-of-speech split.

summary: The structure is sound and the Old Testament material (232-verse place row, the holy/common distinction, the Holy One of Israel row) is handled on its own terms; the Spirit grouping holds, all 89 verses carry the words. It ships after the sanctification grouping is made side-neutral (merge the verb pair, strip the framing from the noun pair, unify the notes, fix the label whose quotation occurs in none of its verses) and the Holy One, holy-ones, place and saints rows are relabelled or reordered as listed.
